title: Coffee Shop
concepts_tested: multi-year DCF valuation vs. asking price
prompt: A friend asked me if I wanted to buy his coffee shop for $100,000. Do you think I should do it?

clarifying_info.answer: The coffee shop is in Vail, Colorado.
Cup of coffee $4.00; bottled water $2.00; pastries $3.00.
The shop serves mostly locals, not tourists, so demand is consistent throughout the year.
Rent was $500/month. Wages (for 2 employees) were $8.00/hour. The shop is open 12 hours a day, six days a week.
Candidate may assume the coffee shop will bring in consistent profits.

interviewer_notes: This is a valuation question — the candidate needs to build up profitability (revenue, costs, taxes) before valuing the business, then compare that valuation to the $100,000 asking price. Share each bullet of information only if the candidate asks for it clearly and deliberately.

suggested_framework.summary: Value the coffee shop as a multi-year discounted cash flow (revenue build from customer traffic → fixed/variable costs → after-tax profit → 5-year DCF at the given WACC) and compare that value to the $100,000 asking price.

tree.label: Should I buy the coffee shop for $100,000?

children.label: Variable cost (50% margin on all products)
5-year discounted cash flow at assumed WACC
Compare DCF value to $100,000 asking price

stages.interviewer_asks: A friend asked me if I wanted to buy his coffee shop for $100,000. Do you think I should do it?
stages.expected_answer: Candidate frames this as a valuation question: first estimate the shop's profitability (revenue less costs and taxes), then value it (e.g., as a multi-year discounted cash flow), and compare that value to the $100,000 asking price.
good_answer_signals: Explicitly frames the problem as 'value the business, then compare to price'
Lays out the revenue → costs → profit → valuation chain before asking for numbers

stages.interviewer_asks: How would you estimate the shop's customer traffic and revenue?
stages.release_when: Only if candidate asks clearly and deliberately
stages.info_to_release: Assume 10 customers/hour in a slow hour and 20 customers/hour in a busy hour; the first and last 2 hours of the day are busy hours; shop is open 12 hours/day, 6 days/week; assume Saturday is entirely busy hours; assume the shop operates roughly 50 weeks/year.
stages.expected_answer: Weekday customers = 20×4 (busy hours) + 10×8 (slow hours) = 160/day. Saturday (all busy) = 20×12 = 240. Customers/week = 160×5 + 240×1 = 1,040. Customers/year ≈ 1,040×50 ≈ 52,000 (book states 50,200, an apparent arithmetic slip — see math log).
good_answer_signals: Splits the day into busy vs. slow hours correctly
Treats Saturday as a distinct, busier day
Annualizes weekly traffic with a reasonable weeks/year assumption

stages.interviewer_asks: Given that traffic, what's the shop's annual revenue?
stages.info_to_release: Assume 60% of customers order coffee ($4), 30% order a pastry ($3), and 10% order bottled water ($2).
stages.expected_answer: Using ~50,000 annual customers (the book's own rounding of its traffic estimate): Revenue = 50,000×60%×$4 + 50,000×30%×$3 + 50,000×10%×$2 = $120,000 + $45,000 + $10,000 = $175,000.
good_answer_signals: Applies the order-mix percentages to price correctly
States and uses a consistent annual-customer figure

stages.interviewer_asks: What are the shop's fixed costs?
stages.info_to_release: Rent $500/month; wages $8.00/hour for 2 employees; open 12 hours/day, 6 days/week, ~50 weeks/year. Candidate can also consider utilities and insurance as additional assumptions.
stages.expected_answer: Rent = $500×12 = $6,000/year. Wages (per the book's own formula) = $8×12hrs×6days×50weeks = $28,800/year (book states $30,000 — see math log). Total fixed costs ≈ $34,800/year (book's figure: $36,000).
good_answer_signals: Annualizes rent and wages from the monthly/hourly inputs
Notes that utilities/insurance could be added as further assumptions

stages.interviewer_asks: So what's the shop's annual profit, before and after tax?
stages.expected_answer: Pre-tax profit = Revenue×50% margin − fixed costs = $175,000×50% − fixed costs ≈ $87,500 − $34,800 ≈ $52,700 (book states $52,500). After-tax profit = pre-tax profit × (1−40%) ≈ $31,600 (book states $31,500).
good_answer_signals: Applies the 50% product margin to revenue before subtracting fixed costs
Correctly applies the tax rate to get after-tax profit

stages.interviewer_asks: Assuming the shop operates for 5 years and using a 10% WACC, what is it worth today?
stages.info_to_release: Assume a 5-year operating horizon and a 10% WACC.
stages.expected_answer: Value ≈ after-tax profit × [1 + 1/1.1 + 1/1.1² + 1/1.1³ + 1/1.1⁴] ≈ $31,500 × 4.17 ≈ $131,000 (using the book's own after-tax profit figure and discounting formula).
good_answer_signals: Discounts a multi-year stream of consistent after-tax cash flows at the given WACC
Arrives at a valuation figure to compare against the $100,000 asking price

stages.interviewer_asks: So, should I buy the coffee shop?
stages.expected_answer: Yes — as long as sales stay consistent over the next 5 years, the estimated value (~$131,000) exceeds the $100,000 asking price, making the purchase profitable. Candidate should flag that further diligence on the seller's management experience and local competition would help confirm the consistent-sales assumption.
good_answer_signals: Explicitly compares the DCF value to the $100,000 asking price to reach a recommendation
Flags at least one real-world risk (competition, management/operational continuity) to the consistent-sales assumption

math.question: How many customers does the shop see per day (weekday)?
givens: First and last 2 hours of the 12-hour day are busy (4 busy hours, 8 slow hours)

math.question: How many customers does the shop see per week and per year?
givens: 160 customers on each of 5 regular days
Saturday treated as all 12 hours busy: 20×12 = 240 customers
math.book_answer_if_different: Book states 1,040 × 50 = 50,200, which is an arithmetic error (1,040 × 50 = 52,000, not 50,200).

math.question: What is the shop's annual revenue?
givens: ≈50,000 annual customers (book's own rounding of its traffic estimate)

math.question: What are the shop's annual fixed costs?
givens: Wages $8.00/hour, shop open 12 hours/day, 6 days/week, ~50 weeks/year
math.book_answer_if_different: Book states wages = $8×12×6×50 = $30,000 (arithmetic error: the formula as given computes to $28,800) and total fixed costs = $36,000.

math.question: What is the shop's pre-tax annual profit?
math.book_answer_if_different: Book states $52,500, which does not exactly reconcile even with the book's own $36,000 fixed-cost figure ($87,500 − $36,000 = $51,500, not $52,500) — an additional apparent arithmetic slip in the book.

math.question: What is the shop's after-tax annual profit?
math.book_answer_if_different: Book states $31,500, derived from its own (also slightly inconsistent) $52,500 pre-tax figure: $52,500 × 60% = $31,500.

math.question: What is the present value of the coffee shop, assuming a 5-year horizon of consistent after-tax profit and a 10% WACC?
givens: After-tax profit ≈ $31,500/year (book's figure, used here since it is the book's own DCF input)
5-year horizon, cash flows in years 0 through 4
math.answer: ≈$131,000 (matches the book's stated valuation); using our recomputed after-tax profit of ≈$31,620 instead gives ≈$131,850 — either way comfortably above the $100,000 asking price

synthesis: Yes, buy the coffee shop. Even after correcting a few small arithmetic slips in the book's own worked solution, the shop's estimated present value (roughly $131,000–$132,000, discounting 5 years of after-tax profit at a 10% WACC) comfortably exceeds the $100,000 asking price, as long as sales stay as consistent as assumed. Before finalizing, it's worth diligencing the seller's management/operational continuity and the local competitive environment to confirm that the 'consistent profits' assumption will hold.
what_great_looks_like: Frames the problem explicitly as 'value the business, then compare to the asking price'
Builds revenue from first principles (traffic by hour-of-day, product mix, pricing) rather than guessing a top-line number
Correctly separates fixed and variable costs and annualizes monthly/hourly inputs
Applies tax and a multi-year discounting approach rather than valuing a single year's profit
Explicitly compares the resulting valuation to the $100,000 ask and flags real-world diligence items (management, competition) behind the consistency assumption
common_pitfalls: Values a single year of profit instead of discounting a multi-year cash flow stream
Forgets to apply the 50% product margin before subtracting fixed costs
Skips taxes entirely when computing the cash flow to discount
Never circles back to explicitly compare the computed value to the $100,000 asking price

extraction.notes: The book's own worked solution contains several small, apparently unintentional arithmetic slips that don't reconcile with its own stated inputs: (1) 1,040×50 is printed as 50,200 instead of 52,000; (2) its wage formula 8×12×6×50 is printed as $30,000 instead of $28,800; (3) its own $87,500−$36,000 is printed as profit $52,500 instead of $51,500. Recomputed each step independently per extraction rule 4 and flagged verified=false with the book's original figures preserved in book_answer_if_different. None of these discrepancies change the final recommendation — the valuation stays well above the $100,000 asking price either way.
